data.title: Memory of Mass Persecution of Armenians and Assyrians in Four Recent Iraqi Novels
data.abstractNote: In recent years, a number of Iraqi intellectuals have participated in a discourse on pluralism in Iraq that includes a call to address the traumatic collective experiences of the country’s ethno-religious minorities. Such a confrontation with the “wounded memory” of these minority groups – along with a rewriting of the modern history of Iraq to incorporate their stories – would be an important step in creating a new collective memory, one of cultural pluralism, that could lead to a true coexistence among all Iraqis. Since it is very difficult to carry out this process due to deep sectarian divisions within Iraqi society, literature provides an alternative cultural field for the deconstruction and reformulation of existing “master narratives”. The purpose of the article is to examine literary representations of the “wounded memory” of minorities in Iraq. The examples used here are related to the 1915–1916 Armenian genocide in the former Ottoman Empire and the 1933 massacre of Assyrians in the northern Iraqi village of Simele. They can be found in the following novels written in Arabic by Iraqi authors of Christian origin: Aṭ-Ṭuyūr al-‘amyā’ (The Blind Birds, 2016) by Laylā Qaṣrānī, Sawāqī al-qulūb (The Streams of Hearts, 2005) by In‘ām Kaǧaǧī, ‘Irāqī fī Bārīs: sīra ḏātiyya riwā’iyya (An Iraqi in Paris: An Autobiographical Novel, 2005) by Ṣamū‘īl Šam‘ūn, and Fī intiẓār Faraǧ Allāh al-Qahhār (Waiting for Farag Allah al-Qahhar, 2006) by Sa‘dī al-Māliḥ. This article is divided into three sections. An introduction is devoted to the aforementioned discourse. The second and solely descriptive section consists of three subsections focusing on literary characters who experience and/ or witness the tragic events and/or tell others about them. The third section contains concluding remarks and refers to several concepts formulated by researchers in cultural memory studies.

data.abstractNote: Christianity gained prominence despite not being the official state religion. The pagan cult persisted, necessitating careful management. In 529, Justinian’s decree made paganism illegal, restricting freedom of conscience. The ecclesiastical structure generally followed the principle of one bishop per city but faced challenges and exceptions. Well-established Christian regions had a dense ecclesiastical network for organization and pastoral care. A confessing Christian community existed before Constantinian times, with monasticism as an extension of early Christianity. Ordinary residents were part of the lay community, and new converts showed diverse levels of zeal. Many converts from paganism retained old rituals due to their cultural differences from the biblical world, leading to engagement in various forms of popular religion.

data.title: Une controverse sur le péché d’origine en Orient au VI<sup>e</sup> siècle
data.abstractNote: «In the beginning of the sixth century, a powerful Christological controversy arose in the non-Chalcedonian party, while it was being persecuted by the Emperor Justinian. This controversy, which opposed Julian of Halicarnassus and Severus of Antioch, officially dealt with the "incorruptibility" of Christ's body during his earthly existence. The actual issue was, in fact, a different conception of the "sin of nature" between the two protagonists. Julian did not make any distinction between sin and corruptibility. For him, real human nature was that of Adam before the fall. Corruption was added to it as from outside. The incarnate Word, being unable to sin, was therefore assuming the original nature of Adam, free from any corruption. The emotions and sufferings he endured were not a necessity, but freely accepted. Redemption was to be achieved in a juridical way: the perfect sacrifice of the incorruptible Word of God redeeming humanity from corruption. Severus offered in opposition to it a dynamic and organic soteriology. Most of all, he made a clear distinction between corruption and sin. The corruption inherited from nature is different from the actual sins which humans commit, and which constitute them as sinners. The Word of God was therefore able to assume our corrupted nature, manifested through the "sinless emotions", though remaining totally free from sin. He was therefore really consubstantial to our nature, uniting us, through it, to his divinity in order to bestow upon us the grace of divinisation. The importance of this sixth century debate will again come to the fore as the theological dialogue between Roman Catholic and Byzantine Orthodox Churches is expected to deal with the controversial issue of the "immaculate conception " of the Virgin Mary.» (Résumé du périodique, p. 23)

data.abstractNote: "Le texte syriaque - et en particulier celui de la Peshitta, est peu cité dans les commentaires. Pourtant il serait dommage de le négliger. [L'A.] montre que celui d'Ephésiens atteste une grande fidélité au texte byzantin, avec pourtant quelques particularités qui ne se trouvent pas forcément dans les variantes grecques, mais qui sont propres au syriaque, comme le mot "amour" mis à la place de "crainte" dans 5/21." (p. 99)
